video_metadata.working_title: COLORADO 1982 Cold Case Solved After 39 Years — Justice for Annette and Bobbie Jo
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: On January 6, 1982, two young women hitchhiking out of Breckenridge, Colorado, were abducted and shot hours apart by the same man, who was rescued from a snowbound mountain pass that same night; a pair of orange socks linked the murders, blood on a glove preserved his DNA, and 39 years later genetic genealogy named Alan Lee Phillips, who was convicted in 2022 and died in prison in 2023.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into stunned disbelief at how close the killer was all along (he was rescued by authorities the same night), then hard-won justice shadowed by later doubts raised over a disgraced DNA analyst

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Alan Lee Phillips (convicted killer; antagonist). Born 1951, died February 27, 2023.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: 30 in January 1982 [12]; 70 at arrest in February 2021 [1][11]; 71 at sentencing in November 2022 [3][4]; 71 at death (some outlets say 72) [31][33]
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Mechanic in 1982 [12]; described in 2021 as a semi-retired mechanic living in Dumont, Clear Creek County, Colorado [19][45]
protagonist.location: Dumont, Clear Creek County, Colorado, at the time of arrest [3][30]
protagonist.physical_description: On the night of January 6, 1982, rescuers noticed a bruised face; he gave explanations (a fall in the snow; hitting his truck) that investigators later rejected [12][17]. No other verified description gathered.
protagonist.background_brief: Arrested in 1973 for assault and burglary, according to Det. Sgt. Wendy Kipple's account of his criminal history [12][46]. On the night of the murders his pickup, without tire chains, became stuck in a drift on Guanella Pass during a snowstorm; he flashed SOS with his headlights, a sheriff aboard a passing airliner saw it, and a fire chief, Dave Montoya, drove up and rescued him [12][15][16]. He told Montoya he had been drinking and decided to drive home [12]. He lived in Colorado for decades afterward without being connected to the killings until 2020-2021 [1].
protagonist.psychological_profile: Not documented by any expert source gathered. Kipple described him as someone who 'wouldn't throw anything away' and 'didn't even throw out his garbage' during surveillance [12][46]. He maintained his innocence, said he would appeal, and claimed the DNA was contaminated and mishandled [3][4]. Do NOT speculate about motive; none was established in sources gathered.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: Semi-retired mechanic in a small mountain town; kept his garbage instead of throwing it out, which slowed the covert DNA collection [12][46].

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Annette Kay Schnee
individuals.role_or_profession: 21-year-old woman, formerly of Sioux City, Iowa, living in the Breckenridge area; born 1960 [25][47]. Occupation not verified.
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Stranger. Picked up while hitchhiking home from Breckenridge to Blue River on January 6, 1982 [25][10].
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Abducted and shot to death; body found July 3, 1982, face down in Sacramento Creek near Fairplay, Park County, about 10 miles south of Hoosier Pass, fully clothed in a blue jacket and wearing one orange sock [13][25][9].
individuals.humanizing_detail: The orange socks were a recent Christmas present from her mother [13]. Her younger sister Cindy French remembered that Annette babysat her: 'She was with me a lot babysitting me' [28]. Her brother Russell is seven years older and still lives in the Siouxland area [28][29].

individuals.name: Barbara 'Bobbie Jo' Oberholtzer (also spelled Bobbi Jo)
individuals.role_or_profession: 29-year-old woman living in Alma, Park County, married to Jeff Oberholtzer [12][25]. Occupation not verified.
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Stranger. Picked up while hitchhiking home from Breckenridge to Alma on the evening of January 6, 1982 [25].
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Shot twice in the chest; found the next day (January 7, 1982 per most sources; January 8 per 48 Hours) hidden by snowbanks a few hundred feet from the top of Hoosier Pass, with an 18-inch zip tie on one wrist [9][46]. Investigators concluded she fought back, likely striking him with a brass key ring; her glove carried his blood [12][14].
individuals.humanizing_detail: She phoned her husband that evening to say she had a ride and would be home relatively soon [12][46].
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: As relayed by Jeff Oberholtzer: she said she'd be home relatively soon and that she had a ride [12].

individuals.name: Jeff Oberholtzer
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Reported his wife missing, found her bloody glove and tissue on the roadside the next day, and lived under suspicion until DNA in the early 1990s showed the blood belonged to an unidentified man [12][19][46]. His business card had been found in Annette Schnee's pocket; he said he had once given it to her when he gave her a ride hitchhiking [19].
individuals.humanizing_detail: Described being 'tried in the court of public opinion' [46].
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: 'It was very painful.' / 'Being under suspicion from not only the authorities, but also being tried in the court of public opinion. People didn't want a suspected murderer in their house.' [46]

individuals.name: The Schnee family: mother (name not verified), brother Russell Schnee, sister Cindy French, another sister
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Six months of not knowing; Cindy French's statement at sentencing described their mother breaking down crying during the months Annette was missing [3][4]. Her mother, brother and two sisters lived to see the conviction [25].
individuals.humanizing_detail: The family retained retired Denver homicide detective Charlie McCormick as a private investigator for one dollar a year [19][20].
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: Cindy French: 'She was with me a lot babysitting me' [28].

individuals.name: Andrea Shelton
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Believes her father was wrongfully convicted; through the Mehr Jolly law firm she gave notice of intent to sue CBI and in June 2025 filed a notice of claim seeking $100 million over former CBI analyst Yvonne 'Missy' Woods' role [34][35][36]. These are allegations; no court finding.

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: Two families (Schnee and Oberholtzer), Jeff Oberholtzer as a long-time suspect, and the wider Colorado justice system later shaken by the Missy Woods DNA scandal
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: Grief, decades of uncertainty, wrongful suspicion, and after the conviction, renewed doubt raised by the defendant's family

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Det. Sgt. Wendy Kipple
characters.role_in_story: Park County Sheriff's Office detective who worked the genealogy lead, the surveillance and the arrest
characters.key_actions_they_took: Received the names Alan and Bruce Phillips; checked criminal history; found a file tab 'Alan Phillips' in old records; ran surveillance; obtained discarded DNA; handcuffed Phillips [12][46]
characters.notable_quotes: 'Halfway back I see this tab, says, "Alan Phillips."' / 'He wouldn't throw anything away.' / 'He didn't even throw out his garbage.' / 'I got to put the handcuffs on him and he was shocked.' / 'The look on his face was just priceless.' [12][46]; 'It was his own stupidity that got him up there, because the pass is not passable in the wintertime' (as reported by the New York Times, via secondary summary; single-sourced) [12]

characters.name: Charlie McCormick
characters.role_in_story: Retired Denver homicide detective; private investigator for the Schnee family
characters.key_actions_they_took: Worked the case for decades (one report: 32 years) for a fee of one dollar a year; described in one headline as an 81-year-old still on the trail [19][20][21]

characters.name: Investigator Eaton (first name not verified)
characters.role_in_story: Stayed on the case for the Summit County Sheriff's Office

characters.name: Jim Hardtke
characters.role_in_story: Colorado Bureau of Investigation agent in 1982
characters.key_actions_they_took: Worked the original scene where the first orange sock was found [13]
characters.notable_quotes: 'It didn't fit anything connected to Bobbie Jo Oberholtzer. It was just one of those mysterious things that you pick up at a crime scene.' [13]

characters.name: Dave Montoya
characters.role_in_story: Fire chief in 1982 who drove up Guanella Pass and rescued Phillips
characters.key_actions_they_took: Rescued Phillips the night of January 6, 1982; later recalled Phillips saying he had gotten drunk and decided to drive home [12]

characters.name: Sheriff Tom McGraw
characters.key_actions_they_took: Announced the arrest at CBI headquarters on March 3, 2021 [1]

characters.name: United Data Connect
characters.role_in_story: Denver genetic genealogy company (founded by former Denver District Attorney Mitch Morrissey) that worked with Metro Denver Crime Stoppers
characters.key_actions_they_took: Extracted DNA from case evidence and traced it through genealogy to two brothers, only one of whom, Alan, had lived in Colorado [1][25][43]

characters.name: Mark Hurlbert
characters.role_in_story: Deputy District Attorney who prosecuted / read victim family statement at sentencing
characters.key_actions_they_took: Read Cindy French's statement at sentencing [3][4]

characters.name: Judge Stephen Broome
characters.key_actions_they_took: Imposed two consecutive life sentences without parole on November 7, 2022 [3][4]

characters.name: Kevin Mehr
characters.role_in_story: Attorney, Mehr Jolly firm, for Andrea Shelton
characters.key_actions_they_took: Filed notice of intent to sue CBI; argued the conviction rested on DNA handled by Missy Woods [34][35][36]
characters.notable_quotes: 'the only evidence against our client was DNA and DNA specifically processed and analyzed by "Missy" Woods' [34][35]

characters.name: Yvonne 'Missy' Woods
characters.role_in_story: Former CBI DNA analyst at the center of a statewide scandal
characters.key_actions_they_took: Analyzed DNA for CBI for 29 years and testified in high-profile trials [40]. Charged with 102 felonies (January 2025); pleaded guilty June 2026 to four felonies; sentenced September 8, 2026 to 10 years [38][40][49]. Her specific role in the Phillips case is alleged by the Phillips family's lawyer; not established by any court in sources gathered.
characters.notable_quotes: 'I know an apology cannot undo the harm' (at sentencing, September 2026) [38]

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Guanella Pass and Hoosier Pass, Colorado Rockies
the_moment.what_is_happening: Two women have vanished from the roadsides of Breckenridge. That same night, on another mountain pass, a man flashes SOS with his truck's headlights; a sheriff on an airliner sees it, and rescuers bring him down.
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: The rescued man was the killer, with a bruised face; 39 years pass before anyone knows.
the_moment.ironic_twist: Authorities saved the killer's life the same night; and an orange sock given as a Christmas present was the clue that tied two murders together.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who picked up two hitchhikers hours apart on the same snowy day, and how did a drop of his blood on a glove wait 39 years to name him?

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Investigative (forensic) genetic genealogy, followed by a covert discarded-DNA confirmation sample
step_by_step_explanation: 1982: blood on Bobbie Jo's glove and tissues is collected and preserved [9][14].
Early 1990s: DNA analysis shows the blood belongs to an unidentified male and excludes Jeff Oberholtzer [19].
2020: Park County, with Metro Denver Crime Stoppers and United Data Connect, extracts DNA from the evidence and builds a genealogy profile [1].
Comparisons with relatives who had shared DNA in genealogy databases lead to a family tree and two brothers: Alan and Bruce Phillips [1][46].
Only Alan had lived in Colorado [1][25].
Kipple checks his record (1973 arrest) and old files [12][46].
Surveillance (one report: 4-5 weeks); a discarded item is collected; its DNA matches the glove blood [1][12][31].
Arrest February 24, 2021; a direct DNA sample is taken and the match is confirmed again [1][19].
the_method.why_it_worked: The killer's blood was preserved on the victim's glove for decades; genealogy databases reach relatives even when the suspect himself was never in a criminal DNA database.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: Using DNA shared with distant relatives who uploaded their DNA to genealogy sites to rebuild a family tree that narrows to one person
DNA left on something a person threw away, which police can collect without a warrant to confirm a lead
A direct comparison between the suspect's DNA and the crime-scene DNA; genealogy alone is only a lead

the_method.scale_of_operation: One preserved bloodstain; two brothers narrowed to one; weeks of surveillance

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Not a single institutional failure; the limits of 1982 forensics, siloed records (a rescue report on another pass the same night was never connected), and a long-wrong suspect. Later: the CBI lab scandal (Missy Woods) cast a shadow over many convictions.
systemic_failure.how_they_were_supposed_to_protect: Investigators were supposed to identify the man who left blood on Bobbie Jo's glove.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: No DNA technology in 1982; the cases were not linked until July 1982; the husband became the focus; the man rescued from Guanella Pass that night was not tied to the murders until genealogy in 2020 [12][17][19].
specific_incompetence_examples: Jeff Oberholtzer lived under suspicion until the early 1990s, when DNA cleared him [19][46].
Phillips was rescued with a bruised face on the night of the murders but was not linked for 39 years [12][17].

Concerns about Missy Woods' work were raised in 2014 and 2018; she was suspended from casework and then reinstated, per an internal affairs report (general CBI context, not specific to this case) [36]/[50].
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The killer's life was saved by an emergency response that same night.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Park County Sheriff's Office, with Summit County Sheriff's Office, Colorado Bureau of Investigation, Metro Denver Crime Stoppers and United Data Connect [1]
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Focus on husband Jeff Oberholtzer; the two cases were not linked until Annette's body was found in July 1982 [13][19]
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: 2020 genetic genealogy pointing to the Phillips brothers [1]
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: His blood on Bobbie Jo's glove, left as she fought back [12][14]

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.location: Near his home, Clear Creek County (traffic stop)
the_confrontation.scene_description: Arrested without incident during a traffic stop; Kipple put the handcuffs on him [1][12][19]
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: He had lived roughly an hour's drive from the crime scenes for decades (general geography; distance not verified - do not state a number).

charges_filed: Initial: 2 counts first-degree kidnapping, 2 counts first-degree assault, 2 counts first-degree homicide [1]
Convicted on 8 counts: first-degree murder after deliberation, first-degree felony murder (kidnapping), first-degree felony murder (robbery) and second-degree kidnapping, for each victim [2][25]
legal_resolution.trial_date_if_applicable: Trial in Fairplay, Park County; verdict September 15, 2022 [2][5]
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Not gathered verbatim. Defense position: DNA contaminated / mishandled [3][4]. Mehr later said Woods' DNA evidence entered at the '11th hour' (allegation) [34].

victim_impact_statements.from_whom: Cindy French, Annette's sister (read by Deputy DA Mark Hurlbert)
victim_impact_statements.key_quote: Described their mother breaking down crying during the six months Annette was missing (paraphrase) [3][4]
victim_impact_statements.emotional_impact: The family's half-year of not knowing

legal_resolution.sentence_received: Two consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole, November 7, 2022 [3][4]
legal_resolution.protagonist_statement_in_court: Said he would appeal, claiming the DNA was contaminated and mishandled [3][4]
legal_resolution.current_status: As of October 2026: Phillips is dead (February 27, 2023; reported suicide). No appellate ruling was found in public reporting; whether a direct appeal was filed or abated was not verified. His daughter's lawyers allege the DNA work was tainted by Missy Woods and filed a $100 million notice of claim (June 2025); no resolution found. Woods was sentenced to 10 years on September 8, 2026. CBI has said it found no evidence that Woods manufactured profiles or planted DNA. No court has vacated or questioned the Phillips conviction in sources gathered.

universal_stakes.why_this_matters_to_viewer: A killer can be hidden in plain sight, even in an official rescue report from the same night.
universal_stakes.how_this_could_happen_to_them: Ordinary trust (accepting a ride in a snowstorm) and an ordinary small-town life.
universal_stakes.lesson_or_warning: Preserve evidence; one glove kept for 39 years gave two families an answer. And forensic labs must be honest, because every conviction depends on them.
universal_stakes.current_relevance: Genetic genealogy keeps solving Colorado cold cases, while the Missy Woods scandal (sentenced September 2026) shows why DNA work must be trustworthy.

next_video_hook.connection_to_current_video: Another case where DNA left at the scene waited decades and genetic genealogy named a man no one had suspected; and where an innocent man (like Jeff Oberholtzer here, though never charged) paid for the investigators' wrong focus, this time with years in prison.
next_video_hook.teaser_line: In Idaho Falls in 1996, an 18-year-old was murdered in her apartment, and a young man went to prison for it. The DNA never matched him. It took a mother's refusal to give up and a family tree to prove it.

notes_and_gaps._instructions: Things you still need to research or verify.
unverified_claims: Cause of Phillips' death: reported as suicide by KTIV (official records) and Denver7/KDVR; the coroner initially said only that no foul play was suspected.
Discovery date of Bobbie Jo: January 7 (most sources) vs January 8 (48 Hours).
Distance of Bobbie Jo's body: about 400 feet from the top (CDAC) vs 300 feet from the parking lot (KKTV).
Confirmation sample: napkin vs Sonic bag vs 'garbage'.
Temperature near -22 F on Guanella Pass: single-sourced.
Kipple's New York Times quote seen only via secondary summary.
Deliberation time: 4 hours vs 5 hours (one summary said five days, clearly an error).
Whether Missy Woods personally processed or testified about the DNA in this case is an allegation by the Phillips family's lawyer; not confirmed by CBI or a court in sources gathered.
Schnee age: 21 in most sources, 22 in some.

Calendar-derived details used in the script: January 6, 1982 was a Wednesday and January 7 a Thursday; February 24, 2021 is 39 years, 1 month and 18 days after January 6, 1982; March 3, 2021 is one week after the arrest; Phillips died 3 months 20 days after sentencing and about 5.5 months after the verdict.

General background used in the script without a fetched source: DNA profiling emerged in the mid-1980s; Golden State Killer arrest announced April 2018; Hoosier Pass crosses the Continental Divide and marks the Summit/Park county line; Ordway lies on the plains of southeastern Colorado.
